lesson.body:
Here's the good news: a great palate isn't something you're born with, it's something you build. Just like your ear can learn to pick out instruments in a song, your nose and mouth get sharper every time you pay attention. So slow down. Take a real sniff before you sip, then notice what you taste and how it feels. That small habit, repeated, is most of the work.

A few simple moves speed things up. Pour two wines and taste them side by side, because differences are far easier to spot than to remember. Build a "smell memory bank" from your kitchen, sniff a strawberry, a lemon, black pepper, fresh herbs, so those scents are ready when a wine reminds you of them. And jot a quick note in the app's journal each time: what you liked, what you didn't.

Don't worry about using fancy words or getting it "right." There are no wrong answers, only your honest impressions. Over time, your notes reveal a map of what you genuinely enjoy, and choosing your next bottle gets easier and more fun.
outcomes: Explain why a palate is built, not born
Use side-by-side tasting and a smell memory bank
Keep honest journal notes about what you enjoy

deep_notes: Much of what you call taste is really smell. Your tongue picks up only a few basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami, a savoury taste. Fruit, spice and oak reach your nose from the back of your mouth, a route called retronasal smell. Pinch your nose while you sip and most of the flavour vanishes. Research suggests experts' main edge is not a sharper nose but a better memory for smells and the words to name them.

Pros call a set of wines tasted together a flight. Change only one thing at a time and the lesson jumps out. Try an unoaked Chardonnay, such as a typical Chablis, next to an oaked one, and the vanilla and toast become obvious. A vertical tasting compares one wine across several vintages (harvest years), while a horizontal tasting compares different wines from the same year.

Many wine smells are the very same molecules found in food. Rotundone, a key part of the smell of black peppercorns, is also behind the peppery note in Syrah. So sniffing real pepper trains you for the wine. Pros sometimes buy aroma kits, small bottles of scents such as blackcurrant or vanilla, but your fridge and spice rack do the same job for free. Sniff with your eyes closed and say the name aloud.

Writing a note forces you to pay attention, and putting a smell into words tends to help you remember it. Add a little context too: the grape, the region, the price and what you ate. Food and mood change how a wine tastes, so a bottle you loved at a sunny lunch may seem different on a cold evening. Patterns in your notes, like always enjoying one grape, are the real prize.

deeper.body: Your nose gets used to a smell fast. After several long sniffs of the same wine, the aroma seems to fade, even though the wine has not changed. Scientists call this olfactory adaptation. Many tasters take two or three short sniffs, pause briefly, then come back to the glass with a fresher nose.
deeper.title: Your nose tires quickly

deeper.body: Palates do differ a little. Some people, often called supertasters, find bitter tastes much stronger than others do. Some cannot smell certain compounds at all: in one well-known study, roughly one in five people tested could not detect rotundone, the peppery compound in Syrah. So a friend whose notes differ from yours may be honest, not wrong.
deeper.title: Not every palate is the same

deeper.q: If a friend cannot smell the pepper in a Syrah, their palate must be untrained.
deeper.why: Some people simply cannot detect rotundone, the peppery compound, and some Syrahs have little of it. So it may have nothing to do with practice.

deeper.body: Labels and prices shape what we taste. In experiments, people have often rated the same wine higher when told it was expensive. Blind tasting, where you taste without seeing the bottle, strips that bias away. Ask a friend to pour two wines into glasses you cannot identify, then guess which is which. It is humbling, fun and one of the fastest ways to sharpen your palate.

v2.body:
A sommelier is a restaurant's wine expert. To pass the tasting part of the **Master Sommelier** exam, one of the hardest tests in wine, you get six unlabelled wines and 25 minutes. For each, you must name the grape, country, region and year. Only a few hundred people have ever earned the title. None of them was born able to do it: they built the skill, usually over years of practice.

Your **palate** is your skill at tasting: noticing what a wine smells, tastes and feels like. Like your ear learning to pick out instruments in a song, your nose and mouth get sharper at noticing every time you pay attention. Take a real sniff before you sip, then notice what you taste and how it feels. That small habit, repeated, is most of the work.

Your nose does most of the tasting, so most palate training is nose training. Research suggests experts usually do not have more sensitive noses than beginners. Their edge is memory: they recognise smells they have met before. So practice trains three things: attention, a memory for smells, and words to name what you notice.

Pour two wines and taste them **side by side**, because differences are far easier to spot than to remember. Small pours are plenty. A set of wines tasted together is called a **flight**, and the best flights change only one thing at a time. Try a Chardonnay pair: one made without oak, such as a typical Chablis from France, next to one aged in oak barrels, and the vanilla and toast of the oak become obvious.

Build a **smell memory bank** from your kitchen. With your eyes closed, sniff a strawberry (a note in light reds such as Pinot Noir), a lemon (many crisp whites), black pepper (Syrah, a red grape) and fresh herbs (many Sauvignon Blancs), and say each name aloud. Then those scents are ready when a wine reminds you of them. Often the link is real chemistry: Australian scientists found that **rotundone**, a key part of the smell of black pepper, is also behind the peppery note in Syrah.

Finally, jot a quick note in the app's journal each time: what you liked, what you didn't, the grape, the region and what you ate. Putting a smell into words tends to help you remember it. No fancy words needed, no getting it "right": there are no wrong answers, only your honest impressions, and they need not match anyone else's. Over time your notes become a **map of your taste**, and choosing your next bottle gets easier and more fun.
deep_notes: The first Master Sommelier exam was held in London in 1969. Besides blind tasting (tasting without seeing the bottle), candidates face a spoken theory exam and a test of restaurant service, and only a small share pass each year. In 2016 a small brain-scan study at the Cleveland Clinic in the United States compared Master Sommeliers with non-experts. Areas linked to smell and memory were larger in the sommeliers, and one was thicker the longer they had worked: a hint that training shapes the brain, even in adults.

The word palate comes from the Latin palatum, the roof of the mouth. That spot was once thought to be where taste lived, so the word came to mean a sense of taste. In wine you hear it two ways: your palate is your tasting skill, and a wine's palate is how it tastes in your mouth, as in 'a fresh palate'. Like learning a language, the skill grows fastest little and often: a few minutes of real attention with each glass.

Not everything you notice in a sip is taste or smell. The warmth of alcohol, the drying feel of tannin (like strong tea) and the weight of the wine, called body, are felt rather than tasted or smelled. Tasters check all three in turn: tastes on the tongue, smells through the nose, then what the wine feels like. Going through them in the same order every time is what turns a vague impression into a useful note.

In a 2002 study from New Zealand, published in the journal Chemical Senses, wine judges and beginners took the same smell tests. The experts were no better at detecting faint smells, and no better at naming them. Where they shone was recognition: they were much better at telling whether they had smelled something before. Years of attentive tasting had built a memory for smells. Nothing in that recipe needs a special nose, which is why the skill is open to anyone.

Memories of smells tend to blur: by next week, last week's wine has faded into a general impression. Two glasses at once let you go back and forth, which is why professionals usually taste wines in flights. Pros who taste many wines in a session spit into a bucket called a spittoon, so their judgement stays clear. At home, small pours and a jug of water do the same job. The aim is to learn, not to drink more.

Pros describe tastings by how the wines line up. A vertical tasting compares one wine across several vintages (harvest years), so you taste how the year and age change it. A horizontal tasting compares different wines from the same year, so the place and the maker stand out. At home the easiest flight is a pair: one grape from two countries, or the same grape with and without oak. Pour them at the same temperature so that is not the difference you notice.

Professionals sometimes buy aroma kits: sets of small bottles holding scents such as blackcurrant, vanilla or cut grass. Your fridge and spice rack do much the same job for free. Sniffing with your eyes closed stops you seeing the answer, and saying the name aloud links the smell to a word. Then go finer: compare an apple with a pear, or a lemon with a lime. Small differences like these are exactly what you will meet in the glass.

Researchers at the Australian Wine Research Institute traced the peppery smell in some Shiraz, as Syrah is called in Australia, to rotundone in 2008. They also showed it is the key peppery smell of peppercorns, and it turns up in herbs such as rosemary and in a few other grape varieties. It comes from the grape and survives fermentation, when yeast turns sugar into alcohol, so what was in the grape reaches your glass. Many wine smells work like this: real chemistry, not just imagination.

Writing a note forces you to pay attention, and putting a smell into words tends to help you remember it. A little context helps too: the grape, the region, the price and what you ate. Food and mood change how a wine tastes, so a bottle you loved at a sunny lunch may seem different on a cold evening. Patterns in your notes, like always enjoying one grape or one region, are the real prize, because they tell you what to try next.

deeper.body: Sensory scientists often train and test tasters with a triangle test. You get three glasses: two hold the same wine, one holds a different wine. Your only job is to find the odd one out, so you need no wine words at all, just attention. Try it at home: ask a friend to pour, out of your sight, two glasses of one wine and one of another, then swap roles.

Some cannot smell certain substances at all: in one well-known study, about one in five people tested could not detect rotundone, the peppery smell in Syrah. So a friend whose notes differ from yours may be honest, not wrong. Training sharpens what you notice, but it starts from the nose and tongue you have.

Price works the same way: in several experiments, people rated the same wine higher when told it was expensive. Blind tasting, where you cannot see the bottle, strips that bias away. steps.remember: Liked it, didn't: that is the note.
steps.why: Honest likes and dislikes build a map of your taste. Fancy words and matching others add nothing.

steps.key: A key part of black pepper's smell is the same substance behind the peppery note in Syrah.
opts: Pepper is added at the winery
It shares a scent with pepper
Its oak barrels add spice
Its yeast makes a peppery smell
steps.q: Why can a Syrah smell like black pepper?
steps.remember: Real pepper trains you for Syrah.
steps.why: The smell is the same chemistry, so sniffing real pepper at home trains you to spot it in the glass.

cards.back: Your skill at tasting: noticing what a wine smells, tastes and feels like. Built, not born.
A set of wines tasted together, side by side; the best change only one thing.
Everyday scents, like lemon or pepper, stored in memory so you recognise them in wine.
A quick, honest note: what you liked, what you didn't, the grape, region and food.
